facts.statement: The animal is classified under the genus Phosphatodraco.
facts.quote: taxon: Phosphatodraco

facts.statement: The genus and species Phosphatodraco mauritanicus were described by Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues in 2003.
facts.quote: authority: Pereda-Suberbiola et al., 2003

facts.statement: Phosphatodraco lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous,

facts.statement: Phosphatodraco was an azhdarchid pterosaur that lived in what is now Morocco during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Phosphatodraco is a genus of azhdarchid pterosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous of what is now Morocco.

facts.statement: A specimen consisting of five cervical vertebrae was discovered in the Ouled Abdoun Phosphatic Basin in 2000.
facts.quote: In 2000 a pterosaur specimen consisting of five cervical (neck) vertebrae was discovered in the Ouled Abdoun Phosphatic Basin.

facts.statement: Phosphatodraco is distinguished by a very elongated C8 (or C7) vertebra that is 50% longer than the C5 and a prominent neural spine almost as tall as the centrum.
facts.quote: Phosphatodraco is mainly distinguished by its C8 (or C7) vertebra being very elongated, 50% longer than the C5, and in having a prominent neural spine that is almost as tall as the centrum

facts.statement: Pterosaur fossils were found in 2000 by the Office Chérifien des Phosphates near Khouribga in central Morocco.
facts.quote: In 2000 pterosaur fossils were found by the Office Chérifien des Phosphates (OCP, located in Casablanca) during paleontological field work in the eastern part of the Ouled Abdoun Phosphatic Basin near the city of Khouribga in central Morocco.

facts.statement: During preparation of the specimen, fossil remains of fish and mosasaurs were found in association.
facts.quote: During mechanical preparation of the specimen fossil remains of other animals were also found in association, including of several types of fish and mosasaurs.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Xabier Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues designated the specimen as the holotype of Phosphatodraco mauritanicus in 2003.
facts.quote: The specimen was made the holotype of the new genus and species Phosphatodraco mauritanicus by paleontologist Xabier Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues in 2003.

facts.statement: At the time of its description, Phosphatodraco was one of the few known azhdarchids with a relatively complete neck and one of the last known pterosaurs.
facts.quote: At the time it was described, it was one of the only known azhdarchids preserving a relatively complete neck (the others being Zhejiangopterus and Quetzalcoatlus), and was one of the last known pterosaurs.

facts.statement: In 2020, Claudio Labita and David M. Martill described an articulated pterosaur wing (specimen FSAC CP 251) assigned to Tethydraco, a genus originally described in 2018 based on a humerus.
facts.quote: In 2020 paleontologists Claudio Labita and David M. Martill described an articulated (where the bones are connected as in life) pterosaur wing from "couche III" (specimen FSAC CP 251, bought from fossil dealers), which they assigned to Tethydraco, a genus also described by Longrich and colleagues in 2018 based on a humerus (upper arm bone).

facts.statement: Labita and Martill concluded that Tethydraco was an azhdarchid and possibly represented the wing elements of Phosphatodraco.
facts.quote: Tethydraco was originally considered a pteranodontid, but Labita and Martill concluded it was an azhdarchid, and that it possibly represented the wing elements of Phosphatodraco.

facts.statement: In 2022, Alexandra E. Fernandes and colleagues recovered Tethydraco as a pteranodontian based on similarities between its humerus and that of Epapatelo.
facts.quote: In 2022 paleontologist Alexandra E. Fernandes and colleagues noted similarities between the humerus of Epapatelo and Tethydraco, and recovered Tethydraco as a pteranodontian.

facts.statement: In 2023, Adele Pentland and Stephen Poropat noted that the deltopectoral crest of FSAC CP 251 is consistent with Azhdarchidae but differs from the Tethydraco holotype.
facts.quote: In 2023 paleontologists Adele Pentland and Stephen Poropat noted that while the hatchet-shaped deltopectoral crest of FSAC CP 251 is consistent with Azhdarchidae, it differs from the shape of the Tethydraco holotype.

facts.statement: There is controversy over the order of the fragmentary holotype cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: Due to the fragmentary nature of the holotype cervical vertebrae, there has been controversy over their order.

facts.statement: Describers considered the vertebrae as C5–C9, while others argue they are C3–C8 with C3 and C4 being distinct vertebrae.
facts.quote: The describers considered them as cervicals (abbreviated as C) C5–C9 in the series, the first preserved vertebra (C5) being broken in two, but others consider them C3–C8, C3 and C4 being two different vertebrae.

facts.statement: The interpretation of the vertebrae affects the estimated size, with describers suggesting a 5 m wingspan versus an alternate interpretation of 4 m.
facts.quote: The interpretation followed has consequences for how Phosphatodraco is distinguished from other azhdarchids and how large it is thought to have been; the describers considered it to have had a wingspan of 5 m; the alternate interpretation would lead to a 4 m wingspan.

facts.statement: It is debated whether azhdarchids like Phosphatodraco were skim-feeders in coastal waters or terrestrial foragers like storks or ground hornbills.
facts.quote: Azhdarchids have historically been considered skim-feeders that caught prey from water in coastal settings, but it has since been suggested that the context in which their fossils are found and their morphology – such as their long, stiffened necks (informed by for example the neck of Phosphatodraco) – is more consistent with them having foraged terrestrially like storks or ground hornbills, but this is still debated.

facts.statement: The diversity of pterosaurs including Phosphatodraco in the late Maastrichtian suggests their extinction happened abruptly 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Although pterosaurs were thought to have declined in diversity towards the time of their extinction 66 million years ago, the diversity in taxa, including Phosphatodraco, in the Ouled Abdoun Basin, which dates to the late Maastrichtian, right before the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event, indicates their extinction happened abruptly.

facts.statement: Researchers originally interpreted the five preserved neck vertebrae of Phosphatodraco as vertebrae C5 through C9.
facts.quote: Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues originally interpreted the five preserved cervical vertebrae of Phosphatodraco as cervicals C5–C9.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Alexander Kellner suggested in 2007 that the original interpretation of Phosphatodraco's vertebrae might have been affected by taphonomy.
facts.quote: In 2007 paleontologist Alexander W. A. Kellner and colleagues noted that Phosphatodraco was one of the most interesting azhdarchids found in Africa, but used cautious language about the original interpretation of the vertebrae.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Alexander Averianov disagreed with Kellner's reinterpretation of the neck vertebrae in 2014, arguing the original description was accurate.
facts.quote: Paleontologist Alexander Averianov disagreed with Kellner's reinterpretation of the cervical vertebrae in 2014, and considered the original description accurate.

facts.statement: Paleontologists Darren Naish and Mark Witton followed Kellner's reinterpretation of the vertebrae order in 2017.
facts.quote: Paleontologists Darren Naish and Mark P. Witton (the co-authors of Vremir's article) followed Kellner's interpretation in 2017.

facts.statement: In 2019, Alexandru Solomon and colleagues noted that even if the reinterpretation of the vertebrae order was correct, the damaged specimen could not be compared with the single known cervical vertebra of the genus Albadraco.
facts.quote: Though the palaeontologist Alexandru A. Solomon and colleagues noted the suggested change in interpretation of the holotype order in 2019, they stated that even if the reinterpretation was correct, the specimen was too damaged for comparison with the single known cervical vertebra of their new genus Albadraco.

facts.statement: In 2003, Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues estimated Phosphatodraco had a wingspan of approximately 5 meters, describing it as a large azhdarchid pterosaur.
facts.quote: In their 2003 description, Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues estimated Phosphatodraco to have had a wingspan close to 5 m, based on comparison with other azhdarchids with preserved cervical vertebrae, and referred to it as a "large azhdarchid pterosaur".

facts.statement: Mark Witton grouped Phosphatodraco with midsized azhdarchids in 2013 based on size estimates.
facts.quote: Witton grouped Phosphatodraco with "midsized" azhdarchids based on this size estimate in 2013.

facts.statement: Following Kellner's interpretation, Naish and Witton listed a neck length of 865 mm and a wingspan of 4 meters for Phosphatodraco in 2017.
facts.quote: Naish and Witton, who followed Kellner's interpretation, listed a neck-length of 865 mm for Phosphatodraco in 2017, and a wingspan of 4 m.

facts.statement: Phosphatodraco was covered with hair-like pycnofibers.
facts.quote: As a pterosaur, Phosphatodraco was covered with hair-like pycnofibers.

facts.statement: Azhdarchids like Phosphatodraco had proportionally long necks and skeletons filled with air sacs that lightened them.
facts.quote: Azhdarchids had necks that were proportionally longer than those of other pterosaurs, and their vertebral column and much of the rest of the skeleton was pneumatized (filled with air-sacs that lightened it).

facts.statement: Azhdarchids had small but robust body skeletons with solidly built upper arm bones.
facts.quote: The body skeleton of azhdarchids was small but robust, and their upper arm bones were solidly built.

facts.statement: Azhdarchids had the largest wing-metacarpals among pterosaurs, which were the longest bones in their wings, while their wing-fingers were relatively short.
facts.quote: Their wing-metacarpals (the hand bones that connect with the fingers) were relatively the largest among pterosaurs, and the longest bones in the wings; their wing-fingers (which supported the wing-membranes) were relatively short.

facts.statement: Kellner's reinterpretation shifted the order of Phosphatodraco's vertebrae to C3 through C8.
facts.quote: Kellner suggested in 2010 that interpretation of the holotype specimen had been affected by taphonomy (changes during decay and fossilisation); he instead proposed that the element originally described as a fifth cervical vertebra was actually the third and fourth vertebrae which had been compressed together, giving the impression that they were a single vertebra broken in the middle. This would shift the order of the vertebrae to C3–C8

facts.statement: The preserved cervical vertebrae of Phosphatodraco have hollow centers with an outer bone layer approximately 1 millimeter thick.
facts.quote: The five preserved cervical vertebrae have hollow centra and their cortical bone (the outer, thick layer) is about 1 mm thick.

facts.statement: The longest preserved cervical vertebra, identified as C5 by Pereda-Suberbiola, was estimated to be about 300 millimeters long when complete.
facts.quote: The longest being the frontmost of those preserved, a C5 broken in two according to Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues (C3–C4 according to Kellner), which they estimated to have been about 300 mm long when complete.

facts.statement: The sixth cervical vertebra is the best-preserved specimen and measures about 225 millimeters in length.
facts.quote: The C6 (Kellner's C5) is the best-preserved of the vertebrae, and is shorter than the preceding C5, about 225 mm long.

facts.statement: The eighth cervical vertebra has a very elongated centrum measuring 150 millimeters, despite missing part of its front section.
facts.quote: The next to last vertebra is C8 (Kellner's C7) which is visible in side view, and despite missing some of the front, the centrum is very elongated, measuring 150 mm.

facts.statement: The eighth vertebra features a tall neural spine that is 40 millimeters high, nearly matching the 45-millimeter height of the centrum.
facts.quote: The most notable feature of this vertebra is its tall neural spine, which is placed at its hindmost part. The neural spine is 40 mm high measured from the upper surface of the postzygapophys to the top, almost the same height as the centrum, which is 45 mm.

facts.statement: The ninth cervical vertebra has a preserved section that is 75 millimeters high.
facts.quote: The last vertebra is the C9 according to Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues (Kellner's C8,) which is visible in hind view, and its preserved part is 75 mm high.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the last two vertebrae might be dorsal vertebrae that have been incorporated into the neck, a phenomenon known as cervicalization.
facts.quote: Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues suggested the C8–C9 could be cervicalized dorsal vertebrae, back vertebrae which have been incorporated into the neck.

facts.statement: Although no cervical ribs are preserved, the structure of the transverse processes suggests the animal likely possessed ribs.
facts.quote: Though none of the vertebrae preserve cervical ribs, the development of the transverse processes of the last vertebra indicates that it probably had ribs.

facts.statement: In 2003, researchers classified Phosphatodraco as an azhdarchid based on elongated cervical vertebrae with low or absent neural spines and specific skull features similar to Quetzalcoatlus and Azhdarcho.
facts.quote: In their 2003 description Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues considered Phosphatodraco a member of Azhdarchidae based on features such as its mid-series cervical vertebrae being elongated, with low vestigial (almost evolutionarily lost) or absent neural spines, the presence of prezygapophyseal tubercles, a pair of lower sulci near the prezygapophyses, and the lack of oval pneumatic foramina on the lower surfaces of the centra.

facts.statement: A 2018 study found Phosphatodraco to be an azhdarchid and the closest relative to Aralazhdarcho from Kazakhstan.
facts.quote: Longrich and colleagues performed a phylogenetic analysis in 2018 that included Moroccan pterosaurs. They found Phosphatodraco to be an azhdarchid and the sister taxon of Aralazhdarcho from Kazakhstan.

facts.statement: In 2021, Brian Andres identified Phosphatodraco and Aralazhdarcho as sister taxa within the azhdarchid subclade Quetzalcoatlinae, supported by reduced pneumatic foramina.
facts.quote: In 2021 American paleontologist Brian Andres also found Phosphatodraco and Aralazhdarcho to be sister taxa, supported by the reduction of pneumatic foramina on the side of the neural canal. This clade was recovered as part of the azhdarchid subclade Quetzalcoatlinae.

facts.statement: A 2022 study by Leonardo Ortiz David and colleagues placed Phosphatodraco and Aralazhdarcho as sister taxa outside the Quetzalcoatlinae subclade, forming a basal group with Eurazhdarcho.
facts.quote: In a 2022 phylogenetic analysis by Argentinian paleontologist Leonardo Ortiz David and colleagues, Phosphatodraco and Aralazhdarcho were again recovered as sister taxa, corroborating their close relationship that is based on similar features. However, unlike Andres in 2021, Ortiz David and colleagues found both pterosaurs outside Quetzalcoatlinae, in a more basal (primitive) position within Azhdarchidae, forming a clade with Eurazhdarcho.

facts.statement: In 2025, a new clade named Phosphatodraconia was defined to include Phosphatodraco, Aralazhdarcho, Eurazhdarcho, and Wellnhopterus based on shared cervical vertebra features.
facts.quote: In 2025, Pêgas and colleagues named the new clade Phosphatodraconia, containing Phosphatodraco, Aralazhdarcho, Eurazhdarcho, and Wellnhopterus, based on cervical vertebra features.

facts.statement: Witton and Naish argued that azhdarchids like Phosphatodraco likely inhabited inland environments and acted as terrestrial stalkers, despite their small, pad-footed feet being unsuited for wading.
facts.quote: Witton and Naish instead stated that azhdarchids probably inhabited inland environments, based on the taphonomic contexts their fossils have been found in (more than half the fossils surveyed were from for example fluvial or alluvial deposits, and most of the marine occurrences also had fossils of terrestrial lifeforms), and their morphology made them ill-suited for lifestyles other than wading and foraging terrestrially, though their feet were relatively small, slender, and had pads, not suited for wading either.

facts.statement: Witton suggested in 2013 that azhdarchids strided through vegetation using long limbs and stiffened necks to spot and grab small animals or fruit from the ground.
facts.quote: Witton elaborated in a 2013 book that the proportions of azhdarchids would have been consistent with them striding through vegetated areas with their long limbs, and their downturned skull and jaws reaching the ground. Their long, stiffened necks would be an advantage as it would help lowering and raising the head and give it a vantage point when searching for prey, and enable them to grab small animals and fruit.

facts.statement: It is debated whether azhdarchids were terrestrial stalkers or aquatic foragers, as some researchers point to marine fossil contexts and the lack of finds in truly terrestrial strata.
facts.quote: Labita and Martill noted that azhdarchids might have been less terrestrial than suggested by Witton and Naish, since the Moroccan fossils were from marine strata, as was Arambourgiania from the phosphates of Jordan. They noted that no azhdarchids had been found in truly terrestrial strata, and proposed they could instead have been associated with aquatic environments, such as rivers, lakes, marine and off-shore settings.

facts.statement: The Late Cretaceous of Morocco holds the most diverse pterosaur assemblage known, including Phosphatodraco, Pteranodontidae, and Nyctosauridae.
facts.quote: Since they found multiple lineages (Pteranodontidae, Nyctosauridae, and Azhdarchidae, the latter including Phosphatodraco and others) to have co-existed during the late Maastrichtian of Morocco, this is the most diverse pterosaur assemblage known from the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the extinction of pterosaurs was abrupt due to the Chicxulub impact, which allowed birds to rapidly evolve and fill their niches.
facts.quote: To these researchers, this indicated that the extinction of pterosaurs was abrupt instead of gradual, caused by the catastrophic Chicxulub impact. Their extinction freed up more niches that were then filled by birds, which led to their evolutionary radiation in the Early Cenozoic.
